migrationNotes: Spine: follow one walker along a corridor. First give a place a number, then the change in place, then the ground covered, then see what survives when the origin moves.
Left out of the lesson (still in the course): phys-measuring-motion-hook, -3, -stretches. Their meaning is covered by other items; -3 became the numeric phys-measuring-motion-origin.

lesson.title: Where did it go?

lead.text: Back in the corridor, we need a way to say where you are with a single number. The trick is to measure from a mark. Choose the door and call it zero, then measure in metres from there, as if a tape measure lay along the floor with its zero end at the door. That starting mark is called the origin, and you can put it wherever suits the job.

A number alone does not say which side of the origin you are on, so we also choose a positive direction. Say it points towards the far end of the corridor. A spot 5 metres along it has the position +5 m. A spot 4 metres behind the door, out in the street, has the position −4 m. The sign gives the side and the number gives how far from the origin.

afterFigure.text: Both choices are ours to make. Two people watching the same walk can pick different origins, or opposite positive directions, and both be right as long as each keeps to their own choice. Once the choices are made, a position is a single signed number. The same idea works up and down: with the ground floor as the origin and up as positive, the basement of a building is a negative position. With that in place we can describe a move from one place to another.

lead.text: Now let the walk begin. You start at the door, which is position 0. You finish at the 5 m mark. That is a change in position. Subtract the starting position from the finishing one and you have its size and its direction, which physics calls the displacement.

Try it on a walker who goes from 1 m to 4 m. Finishing minus starting is 4 − 1 = +3 m. The plus sign says the walker moved towards larger positions, which is our positive direction. The 3 says by how much. If the same walker goes back from 4 m to 1 m, the sum is 1 − 4 = −3 m. The size is unchanged and the sign flips, because the move now goes the other way.

afterFigure.text: Look at what the sum uses. It takes the place where the walker began and the place where it finished, and nothing in between. A walker who took a long route and came back gets the same displacement as one who walked straight there. That makes displacement a tidy answer to where something ended up compared with where it began. How much ground a trip covers needs more than its two ends, and we come to that after some practice.

lead.text: A dot slides along a track from the 2 m mark to the 9 m mark. Right is the positive direction.

reveal.text: You subtracted the start from the finish: 9 − 2. The plus sign says the dot moved in the positive direction.

lead.text: Now run the same sum when the move goes the other way, and keep the sign.

Go back to the walk that opened the lesson: 5 metres along the corridor, then 2 metres back. Its displacement is 3 − 0 = +3 m, since you finished at the 3 m mark and began at 0. A pedometer in your pocket would give a different total, because it counts every step in either direction. It would show 7 metres.

That second number is the distance: the total length of the path you followed. To find it, cut the path wherever you turn round, take each stretch as a plain length and add them up. The 5 m out and the 2 m back both count, and turning round gives no refund for the way back. Distance has no direction, so it is never negative.

afterFigure.text: So one trip has two honest descriptions. Displacement compares where you finished with where you began, and it can be positive, negative or zero. Distance adds up the ground covered, and it can only grow as the trip goes on. The two have the same size only when the trip never turns round. The picture sets a trip that doubles back beside one that goes straight, so you can compare them.

cases.label: Out and back: 0 m, 5 m, then 3 m

steps.headline: A trolley goes from 1 m to 5 m, then back to 2 m. Find its displacement and its distance.

workedSteps.text: Displacement uses only the ends: finish minus start.
Distance adds the stretches. The way out runs from 1 m to 5 m.
The way back runs from 5 m to 2 m, which is 3 m. Add the two stretches.

steps.headline: A cart goes from 1 m to 7 m and back to 1 m. What distance does it cover?

workedSteps.text: The way out runs from 1 m to 7 m.
The way back is the same length.

lead.text: One more check on our measuring set-up: does the choice of origin change the answers? Two friends watch the same walker. One lays a tape with its zero at the door. The other lays a second tape with its zero 10 metres behind the door, so every position she reads is 10 m larger than the first friend's.

Suppose the walker goes from the 3 m mark to the 8 m mark on the first tape. The second tape reads 13 m and 18 m for the same two places. Every reading has shifted by 10, yet the displacement is 8 − 3 = 5 m on one tape and 18 − 13 = 5 m on the other. The shift appears in both terms of the subtraction, so it cancels.

afterFigure.text: This is why we can put the origin wherever it makes the sums easiest. A single position only means something once you know where the origin was, whereas a displacement is the same for everyone who watches the trip. Distance agrees for everyone too, because it is a length along the path and the path does not care where the tape starts.

lead.text: Two students record one trip. The first reads it as 2 m to 9 m. The second has her zero 10 m behind the first student's zero, so each of her readings is 10 m larger.
A robot drives along a straight track and turns round partway.

reveal.text: The robot's displacement is only +3 m, yet it covered 13 m. The turn makes the two numbers differ.

lesson.orientation: Distinguish a change in position from the total distance travelled.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Picture a long straight corridor with a door at one end. You step out through that door and walk 5 metres along the corridor. Then you remember something you left behind, turn round and walk 2 metres back. A friend waiting at the door has watched the whole thing.

Ask the friend two questions and you get two different answers. Ask how much ground your feet covered and they will say 7 metres, the sum of the two walks. Ask where you are now and they will point at a spot 3 metres from the door, without counting the steps that got you there.
Physics gives these two answers separate names so they never get mixed up. We'll follow this walk to see what each one measures and why you need both.

intro.promise: By the end you'll tell a change in position from the distance travelled, and give the change a sign.
intro.whyItMatters: Every later idea about motion starts from where things are and how that changes.

recap.keyIdea: Displacement is final position minus initial position, with a sign. Distance adds every stretch of the path.

blocks.text: You found that 5 m out and 2 m back leaves you 3 m from the door after 7 m of walking. You also saw that moving the origin changes every position but leaves the displacement alone.

recap.nextHook: Nothing in the corridor has a clock yet. Next we time the walk and ask how quickly the position changes.

questions.prompt: A dot moves along a track from the 2 m mark to the 9 m mark, with right positive. What is its displacement in metres?
hints: Locate the starting and finishing coordinates.
Subtract the start from the finish.
Calculate 9 − 2.
questions.onCorrect: +7 m. Final minus initial: the size is how far it moved and the plus sign says which way.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two readings. Displacement is a difference: final minus initial.
The size is right, but the sign is not. It moved towards larger positions.

questions.prompt: A cart goes from 1 m to 7 m and back to 1 m. What total distance does it travel, in metres?
hints: Count both stretches of the trip.
Each stretch has length 7 − 1 metres.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: It travels 6 m out and 6 m back, for 12 m.

questions.onCorrect: 12 m. Distance adds every stretch of the path, so the trip back counts as well as the trip out.

misconceptions.feedback: That is how far the cart ended from where it began. Distance counts every stretch it travelled.
That is the trip out only. The cart also has to come back.

questions.prompt: The origin shifts so that a trip from 2 m to 9 m is recorded as 12 m to 19 m. What happens to the displacement?
hints: Compare the differences between the two pairs of endpoints.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Both readings increase by 10 m; their difference stays +7 m.

questions.onCorrect: It stays the same. Both readings rise by the same amount, so their difference does not change.

misconceptions.feedback: Only the readings change, not the trip. Both ends move by the same amount, so the gap between them does not grow.
Nothing in the trip doubled. Compare the gap between the two readings in each pair.

questions.prompt: A robot moves from 0 m to 8 m, then back to 3 m. How far does it travel altogether, in metres?
hints: Break the trip at the turning point.
The return stretch runs from 8 m to 3 m.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The path has lengths 8 m and 5 m: 8 + 5 = 13 m.

questions.onCorrect: 13 m. Break the trip at the turning point and add the two stretches.

misconceptions.feedback: That is how far the robot ended from where it began. The distance counts the whole path.
That is the trip out only. The robot also travels back.
That is the return stretch only. Count the trip out as well.

questions.prompt: A lift's marked position changes from 5 m to −4 m. With upward positive, find its displacement in metres.
hints: Keep the minus sign on the final position.
Subtract the initial position from the final position.
Calculate −4 − 5.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Final minus initial gives −4 − 5 = −9 m, downward.

questions.onCorrect: −9 m. Final minus initial gives a negative number when the move is in the negative direction.

misconceptions.feedback: The size is right, but the lift went down. With upward positive, a downward move needs a minus sign.
That adds the two readings. Take the start away from the finish.

questions.prompt: A cart travels from −2 m to 4 m and then to 1 m. Which statement describes its trip?
hints: Use endpoints for displacement and both path lengths for distance.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Its displacement is 1 − (−2) = 3 m. Its distance is 6 + 3 = 9 m.

questions.onCorrect: Displacement compares the ends: 3 m. Distance adds both stretches: 9 m.

misconceptions.feedback: These are swapped. The ends give the displacement, and the whole path gives the distance.
The cart finishes at a larger position than it started, so its displacement is not negative.

questions.prompt: How far from the door are you, in metres?
hints: Draw the door as 0 and the first walk as a line going out.
The second walk goes back along the same line.
Take the 2 m back off the 5 m.
questions.onCorrect: 3 m. The second walk undid part of the first. Physics keeps track of position this way.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two walks. The second walk goes the other way, so it takes you back towards the door.

questions.prompt: A marker moves from 6 m to 2 m along a track, with right positive. What is its displacement in metres?
hints: Which reading is the finish, and which is the start?
Displacement is the finish minus the start.
Take the 6 away from the 2.
questions.onCorrect: −4 m. It moved towards smaller positions, so the displacement is negative.

misconceptions.feedback: The size is right, but the marker moved the negative way. The sign has to show that.
That adds the two readings. Displacement is a difference: finish minus start.

questions.prompt: A walker goes 4 m right, then 4 m left. What total distance does the walker cover, in metres?
hints: How long is each stretch?
Distance adds each stretch, pointing either way.
Add the two stretches.
questions.onCorrect: 8 m. Distance never cancels: every stretch adds to it, whichever way it points.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the net change in position. Distance counts both stretches.
That is one stretch. The walker covers two.

questions.prompt: Why does the 5 m turning point not appear in the displacement?
hints: Read each choice against the situation before you answer.

acceptedIdeas: Displacement compares only the start and the finish.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Displacement compares only the start and the finish.

choices.label: Displacement compares only the start and the finish.
The trolley never really reached 5 m.
Turning points are always ignored in physics.

questions.onCorrect: Displacement depends on the two ends only. What happens in between does not change it.

misconceptions.feedback: It did reach 5 m: that is where it turned round. The question is why that point does not enter the sum.
Turning points matter for distance. They are only absent from displacement because of what displacement compares.

questions.prompt: A runner goes from −4 m to 2 m, then on to −3 m. What total distance does the runner cover, in metres?
hints: Break the run at the turning point.
The first stretch is from −4 m to 2 m.
Add 6 and the length of the second stretch.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The stretches are 6 m and 5 m: 6 + 5 = 11 m.

questions.onCorrect: 11 m. Split the run where it turns, then add the lengths of the two stretches.

misconceptions.feedback: That is how far the runner ended from the start. Distance counts the whole path.
That is the first stretch only. Add the stretch back.

questions.prompt: One student reads a trip as 2 m to 9 m. A second student's zero sits 10 m behind the first student's, so she reads 12 m to 19 m. What displacement does the second student find, in metres?
hints: What are the second student's starting and finishing readings?
Displacement is the finishing reading minus the starting one.
Take 12 away from 19.
questions.onCorrect: +7 m. Moving the origin adds the same amount to both readings, so the displacement does not change.

misconceptions.feedback: 10 m is the gap between the two zeros. The walker's move is the gap between its own two readings.
That is the finishing reading on its own. Take the starting reading away from it.

citations.claim: A position is a signed number measured from a chosen origin, with one direction chosen as positive.
Displacement is final position minus initial position, and its sign shows the direction of the move.
Moving from 2 m to 9 m gives a displacement of 9 − 2 = +7 m.
Moving from 6 m to 2 m gives a displacement of 2 − 6 = −4 m.
Distance is the total length of the path, found by adding every stretch, and it is never negative.
For a trolley going 1 m to 5 m and back to 2 m, the displacement is +1 m and the distance is 7 m.
A cart going 1 m to 7 m and back to 1 m travels 6 + 6 = 12 m.
Moving the origin shifts every position by the same amount, so displacement and distance are unchanged.
Readings of 12 m and 19 m give the same displacement as readings of 2 m and 9 m, which is +7 m.
A robot going 0 m to 8 m and back to 3 m covers 8 + 5 = 13 m with a displacement of +3 m.
19 − 12 = +7 m, the same as 9 − 2.
Displacement = 9 − 2 = +7 m.
It travels 6 m out and 6 m back, for 12 m.
The path has lengths 8 m and 5 m: 8 + 5 = 13 m.
Final minus initial gives −4 − 5 = −9 m, downward.
Its displacement is 1 − (−2) = 3 m. Its distance is 6 + 3 = 9 m.
Displacement compares only the start and the finish.
The stretches are 6 m and 5 m: 6 + 5 = 11 m.
The two lengths are 8 m and 5 m, totalling 13 m.
